actions.name: Review blood pressure readings
actions.result: Clinic BP 155/110 mmHg on two separate readings this visit; patient-reported home cuff readings this week ranging 148-158/100-112 mmHg.

actions.name: Measure/record height, weight, calculate BMI
actions.result: Height 5'2" (157.5 cm), weight 178 lb (80.7 kg), BMI 34.0 kg/m2 (Class I obesity). Weight up 8 lb over past 6 months.

actions.name: Review HbA1c
actions.result: HbA1c 8.5% (goal <7% for most adults with T2DM) — indicates uncontrolled diabetes.

actions.name: Review lipid panel
actions.result: Total cholesterol 230 mg/dL (H), LDL 115 mg/dL (borderline-high), Triglycerides 190 mg/dL (H).

actions.name: Review basic metabolic panel (sodium, potassium, BUN, creatinine)
actions.result: Sodium 138 mEq/L (normal), Potassium 4.5 mEq/L (normal, upper range), BUN 16 mg/dL (normal), Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (normal) — renal function currently preserved.

actions.name: Perform 24-hour dietary recall / diet history
actions.result: Patient reports: coffee only or skipped breakfast; lunch often a packed sandwich with deli meat and chips, or fast food grabbed on the way; dinner is the largest meal, often a family-style traditional dish (e.g., kielbasa, pierogis, pickled vegetables, or canned soup) with bread; frequent salty snacking in the evening; limited vegetables and fruit; portions are large at dinner.

actions.name: Assess fluid intake pattern
actions.result: Patient reports drinking mostly tap water and tea but intentionally limiting fluids during the workday due to concern about frequent bathroom trips; reports waking at night to urinate.

actions.name: Review medication list and refill history
actions.result: Amlodipine 5 mg once daily; last 90-day refill history shows pickup consistent with roughly 70% of expected doses filled over past 3 months. Metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals; pharmacy records show patient has been requesting refills at a rate consistent with approximately half the prescribed 1000 mg/day dose over the past 2 months.

actions.name: Screen for edema and venous changes (patient self-exam via camera)
actions.result: Patient shows bilateral ankle swelling on camera; indents when she presses with a finger (pitting). Visible surface veins noted on lower legs.

actions.name: Review physical activity pattern
actions.result: Sedentary desk job; walks only to car/bus; no structured exercise; reports joint/low back pain limiting activity tolerance.

actions.name: Review home blood glucose log (if available)
actions.result: No home glucose monitoring log on file; patient has not been checking blood sugar at home.

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage of change assessment
actions.result: Patient scores in the 'Preparation' stage: acknowledges need to change, has thought about specific steps, but has not consistently acted; expresses high motivation mixed with feeling overwhelmed.

actions.name: Review insurance/coverage status
actions.result: Active Medicaid coverage; may be eligible for nutrition counseling visits and diabetes self-management education (DSME) referral under current plan.

actions.name: Food security screening (e.g., Hunger Vital Sign)
actions.result: Patient endorses 'sometimes true' to worrying food would run out before money for more; denies skipping meals due to lack of money at this time.

actions.name: Review full vital signs panel
actions.result: Temp 98.6°F, HR 78 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 99%, BP 155/110 mmHg, respiratory effort unlabored.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium and energy intake related to limited nutrition-related knowledge and cultural/financial/time barriers, as evidenced by elevated BP (155/110), HbA1c 8.5%, BMI 34, and reported frequent intake of processed/high-sodium traditional and convenience foods.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive sodium intake (NI-5.10.2) related to limited understanding of sodium sources and cultural food pattern, as evidenced by frequent intake of processed meats, canned soups, pickled foods and BP 155/110 mmHg.
Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive energy intake (NI-1.3) related to large evening portions and skipped breakfast leading to compensatory intake, as evidenced by 8 lb weight gain in 6 months and BMI 34.
Nutrition diagnosis: Food- and nutrition-related knowledge deficit (NB-1.1) related to confusion about sodium vs. salt and carbohydrate counting, as evidenced by patient's own statements.
Consider secondary contributor: medication non-adherence (self-reduced metformin dose, inconsistent amlodipine refills) worsening glycemic and BP control independent of diet alone.
keyFindings: Bilateral pitting ankle edema, consistent with amlodipine side effect and/or dietary sodium
Diet high in processed/traditional salty foods, skipped breakfast, large evening meals
Self-reported fluid restriction during workday despite polyuria/polydipsia
Medication adherence gap: metformin self-reduced, amlodipine refill pattern ~70% of expected
Confusion between 'sodium' and 'salt', low health literacy around nutrition labels
Positive food insecurity screen (worry about running out of food)
plan: Education: clarify sodium vs. salt in simple terms (salt is ~40% sodium by weight; focus on reading 'sodium' line on labels) using teach-back.

Collaborative goal-setting: start with one specific, feasible swap (e.g., rinse canned soups/vegetables, choose lower-sodium deli meat, limit added salt at table) rather than eliminating traditional foods.

Discuss preserving cultural food identity: offer lower-sodium preparation tweaks for family recipes (e.g., herbs/spices instead of added salt, smaller portion of traditional dish paired with vegetables) rather than banning them.
Address breakfast skipping and meal timing to reduce large compensatory dinner portions; suggest a simple, affordable breakfast option.
Discuss fluid intake safety: encourage adequate hydration during the day; explain polyuria is from elevated glucose, not from drinking water, and reassure that restricting fluids is not protective.

Flag medication adherence/dosing concerns found on refill review to PCP/pharmacist for medical management; explain how consistent metformin dosing and antihypertensive adherence work together with diet to control glucose/BP.

Address food cost and food insecurity: discuss budget-friendly lower-sodium options, provide referral information for Medicaid-covered diabetes self-management education (DSME) and community food resources (e.g., SNAP, food pantry, farmers market vouchers if available).
Encourage low-impact physical activity given joint/back pain (e.g., short walks, chair exercises) in small increments.
Set one or two SMART, patient-chosen behavioral goals for follow-up (e.g., swap one processed snack daily, track breakfast 4x/week).
Arrange follow-up visit to reassess diet adherence, weight, BP log, and reinforce education; coordinate with PCP regarding medication adjustment given refill/dosing gaps.
Document ADIME note; communicate nutrition diagnosis and plan to interprofessional team (PCP, possibly social work for financial/food assistance).
redFlags: Stage II hypertension (155/110) with symptoms (headache, blurred vision) warrants prompt medical follow-up — not solely a nutrition issue.
Self-reduced metformin dosing and inconsistent antihypertensive refills are a safety concern requiring communication with prescribing provider.

Bilateral pitting edema and venous distension should be medically evaluated (could reflect amlodipine side effect, poorly controlled hypertension, or early cardiovascular/renal strain) even though current renal labs are normal.
Reported fluid restriction behavior in the setting of polyuria/polydipsia and uncontrolled diabetes could worsen dehydration/hyperglycemia and should be addressed.
educationPoints: Sodium is a mineral; salt (sodium chloride) is the most common dietary source — label reading should focus on the 'sodium' value in mg, not just the word 'salt'.
Processed, canned, and pickled foods are major hidden sodium sources even when they don't taste 'salty'.
Traditional/cultural foods do not need to be eliminated — portion size, preparation method, and frequency can be adjusted to fit cultural identity while improving health.
Skipping breakfast can contribute to overeating later in the day; consistent meal timing supports both weight and glucose management.
Restricting water intake does not reduce urination caused by high blood sugar; adequate hydration is safe and important.
Taking medications exactly as prescribed, and reporting side effects rather than self-adjusting doses, helps the care team find a regimen that controls symptoms without compromising control.
Small, specific, sustainable changes are more effective and less overwhelming than trying to overhaul the whole diet at once.

facts.chart: Referred for nutrition counseling after new HTN diagnosis and uncontrolled T2DM
facts.says: My doctor sent me here because my blood pressure and my sugar are both high and she says I need to change what I'm eating.

facts.chart: Reports fatigue, frequent urination, mild headaches, occasional blurred vision
facts.says: I've been so tired lately, and I'm up all night going to the bathroom. Sometimes my head hurts and my eyes get blurry for a bit.

facts.chart: States confusion distinguishing sodium from salt on food labels
facts.says: Honestly I don't really get the difference between sodium and salt - aren't they the same thing? The labels confuse me.

facts.chart: Full-time state employee; reports limited time for meal preparation
facts.says: I work full time at a desk job, and by the time I get home I just don't have the energy or time to cook something fancy.

facts.chart: Diet is mix of traditional Eastern European dishes and convenience/processed foods
facts.says: We eat a lot of the foods I grew up with - kielbasa, pierogis, that kind of thing - plus whatever's quick, like canned soup or something from the drive-through.

facts.chart: Wants explanation for why diet/medication changes are necessary
facts.says: I just want someone to actually explain to me WHY I have to change all this, not just tell me to do it.

facts.chart: Skips breakfast or has only coffee; packed/grabbed lunch; largest meal at dinner with family
facts.says: Breakfast is usually just coffee, I'm rushing out the door. Lunch I pack something or grab fast food. Dinner's the big meal with the family.

facts.chart: Frequent evening snacking on salty processed snacks (chips, pretzels)
facts.says: At night when I'm watching TV I'll go through a bag of chips or pretzels without even thinking about it.

facts.chart: Regularly consumes canned soups, processed/cured meats, pickled vegetables
facts.says: We always have canned soup in the pantry for a quick dinner, and I love pickled vegetables and cold cuts, we always had those growing up.

facts.chart: Expresses concern about affordability of healthier foods
facts.says: Fresh vegetables and the lean meats, that stuff adds up fast. It's cheaper to buy the canned stuff and the processed meat, honestly.

facts.chart: Married; husband supportive, helps with finances and chores, drives her to appointments
facts.says: My husband's really good about helping out, he drives me everywhere and he's been trying to help with meals too.

facts.chart: Reports significant stress balancing work and family responsibilities
facts.says: Between work and now helping out more with my grandchild, I feel stretched pretty thin lately.

facts.chart: Sedentary job; limited structured exercise; low back pain limits activity
facts.says: I sit at a desk all day, and with my back the way it is, I don't really do any exercise on top of that.

facts.chart: Intentionally limits fluid intake during workday due to concern about frequent urination
facts.says: I get thirsty but I try not to drink too much water at work because then I'm running to the bathroom every few minutes.

facts.chart: Reports taking amlodipine most days but occasionally forgets or skips
facts.says: I take my blood pressure pill most days, I just forget sometimes, or honestly sometimes I skip it on purpose.

facts.chart: Avoids amlodipine some days due to fear of leg swelling
facts.says: That pill makes my legs swell up sometimes, so if my legs already feel puffy I just won't take it that day.

facts.chart: Reports taking metformin most days as prescribed
facts.says: I take my sugar pill twice a day like I'm supposed to, with meals.

facts.chart: Admits to reducing metformin dose on her own due to GI upset, without consulting provider
facts.says: Okay, honestly... sometimes I only take half of it. It was giving me really bad stomach problems, so I started cutting it down myself. I didn't tell the doctor.

facts.chart: Feels cutting traditional foods would mean losing cultural/family connection
facts.says: If I stop eating the foods my mother made, it feels like I'm losing a piece of my family, you know?

facts.chart: Reports family pressures her to eat traditional high-sodium dishes at gatherings
facts.says: At family get-togethers everyone pushes food on you, and if I say no it's like I'm insulting my mother-in-law's cooking.

facts.chart: Feels embarrassed discussing her weight and lifestyle habits
facts.says: I'm kind of embarrassed to even talk about my weight, I know I've let it get out of hand.

facts.chart: Sometimes lies down mid-day due to fatigue
facts.says: Some afternoons I just have to lie down for a bit, I don't tell people that, I feel like I should be able to push through.

facts.chart: Buys cheaper, high-sodium processed foods due to tight household budget
facts.says: Between you and me, a lot of what we buy is the cheap canned and processed stuff because the budget's tight some months.

facts.chart: Believes healthy eating is inherently unaffordable
facts.says: Eating healthy just seems like it's for people with money, honestly.

facts.chart: Believes weight loss requires starvation/extreme restriction
facts.says: Isn't losing weight basically just starving yourself? That's what it seems like from what I've read.

facts.chart: Feels providers focus only on numbers, not how she feels day to day
facts.says: Sometimes it feels like the doctors just care about the numbers on the chart, not how I'm actually feeling.

facts.chart: Motivated by desire to be present for grandchild and reduce fatigue
facts.says: I want to be around and have energy to keep up with my grandbaby, that's really what's pushing me.

facts.chart: Drinks 1-2 glasses of wine on weekends; denies other substance use
facts.says: I'll have a glass or two of wine on the weekend, that's about it. No smoking, nothing like that.

facts.chart: No additional family history volunteered beyond current household details
facts.says: My mom actually had some of the same issues, high blood pressure and sugar, later in her life.

facts.chart: Reports GI upset previously associated with metformin
facts.says: That metformin gave me a really upset stomach when I first started it, cramping and all that.

facts.chart: Tends a small home vegetable garden as a hobby
facts.says: I actually have a little garden out back, I grow some tomatoes and peppers, it's one of the few things that relaxes me.

facts.chart: Has a pet dog
facts.says: We've got a dog, Max, he keeps me company and gets me walking at least a little bit.

facts.chart: History of involvement with local political/community groups
facts.says: I used to be pretty active in local community meetings, political stuff, back when I had more free time.

facts.chart: Drinks tea most evenings; avoids sugary drinks
facts.says: I like a cup of tea in the evening to wind down, no sugar in it though, I stay away from soda and juice.

facts.chart: Does not regularly monitor blood pressure at home
facts.says: I don't really check my blood pressure at home, I don't have a cuff.

mismatches.patientClaim: I take my sugar pill twice a day like I'm supposed to, with meals.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows metformin pickups averaging ~30 tablets/month over the past 2 months, consistent with roughly half the prescribed twice-daily (60 tablets/month) regimen.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Reported adherence can differ from pharmacy refill/fill data; when a mismatch is found, explore it with curiosity and without judgment (the hidden fact f18 reveals she self-reduced the dose due to GI side effects) rather than assuming the patient is being untruthful.

mismatches.patientClaim: I take my blood pressure pill most days, I just forget sometimes, or honestly sometimes I skip it on purpose.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows amlodipine pickups at approximately 70% of expected monthly supply over the past 3 months, consistent with intermittent nonadherence.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Refill records can corroborate a patient's self-report of inconsistent adherence; use this concordant finding to open a nonjudgmental conversation about the specific reason (fear of leg swelling, fact f16) rather than simply restating the adherence problem.

objectives.text: Gather a comprehensive nutrition-focused health history and assess the patient's baseline health literacy, including her understanding of sodium versus salt.
Obtain and interpret anthropometric data, vital signs, and relevant laboratory values to characterize nutritional and metabolic status.
Elicit a detailed 24-hour diet recall and meal pattern, identifying specific high-sodium and high-calorie food sources and cultural/financial drivers.
Formulate an appropriate PES (Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms) nutrition diagnosis statement integrating diet history, labs, and anthropometrics.
Identify and reconcile a discrepancy between patient-reported medication adherence and objective refill/pharmacy records, exploring the underlying reasons with nonjudgmental inquiry.
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's ambivalence, cultural attachment to traditional foods, and readiness to change, eliciting personally meaningful motivators.
Identify practical barriers (financial, time, cultural, physical) to dietary change and collaboratively problem-solve small, sustainable, culturally respectful interventions.
Recognize indications for interprofessional referral (e.g., PCP for medication adherence/dosing concerns, diabetes self-management education, social work/community food resources).

patient.name: Yvette Armstrong
patient.appearance: Joining the video call from her kitchen table at home, wearing work clothes as if just home from the office. Posture is a bit slumped with visible tiredness around her eyes; she has a warm, earnest expression and leans toward the camera when trying to understand something. A mug of tea is visible nearby.

persona.personality: Curious, earnest, hardworking, and eager to please, but easily overwhelmed by technical or lengthy explanations. Has a dry sense of humor when she relaxes.
persona.communicationStyle: Asks clarifying questions when confused, sometimes apologizes for asking too many questions. Opens up more when she feels heard rather than lectured. Uses plain, everyday language.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious about her health numbers and a little embarrassed, but hopeful that this visit might finally help things make sense.
persona.background: Grew up in a close-knit Eastern European American family where food was central to every holiday and gathering; now works full-time as a state employee, married with two adult children nearby and one grandchild she adores. Tends a small backyard garden and has a dog named Max. Was once active in local community/political meetings but has less free time now.
speechExamples: Wait, so sodium and salt aren't the same thing? Nobody ever explained that to me.
I feel like every time I turn around there's some new rule about what I can't eat.
I'm not trying to be difficult, I just... I don't want to lose the food that reminds me of my mom.
Can you just tell me straight - am I going to end up like my mother?
Honestly, between work and the grandbaby, some days I just want to sit down and not think about any of this.
concerns: Fear of having a stroke or heart attack like she worries her mother was headed toward
Worry about the cost of 'healthy' food on a tight budget
Fear of disappointing her family by changing traditional recipes
Confusion about conflicting or complicated medical advice
Worry about medication side effects, especially leg swelling

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit with Yvette Armstrong, a 64-year-old woman referred for nutrition counseling due to new Stage II hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. She was referred by her primary care provider for comprehensive nutrition assessment and counseling. Review the chart, conduct a nutrition-focused history and assessment, and provide patient-centered education and goal-setting using motivational interviewing.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral for nutrition counseling due to new Stage II hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me - my doctor said I really need to talk to someone about my eating because my blood pressure and my sugar are both pretty high right now.
tasks: Conduct a nutrition-focused history including 24-hour diet recall, meal pattern, and psychosocial/cultural context
Review relevant anthropometrics, vitals, and laboratory data with the patient
Review the medication list with the patient
Assess readiness to change and identify nutrition-related concerns
Use motivational interviewing to deliver culturally respectful, literacy-appropriate education and develop a collaborative action plan
Document the encounter using the ADIME format

profile.summary: This case presents a 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Stage II hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes referred for an initial outpatient nutrition assessment via telehealth. It teaches diet-focused history taking, interpretation of anthropometric and lab data, recognition of a patient-reported vs. pharmacy-record medication adherence mismatch, and culturally sensitive, health-literacy-appropriate motivational interviewing and goal-setting.
profile.title: Uncontrolled Hypertension and Type 2 Diabetes in a 64-Year-Old Woman: Nutrition Assessment and Culturally-Responsive Counseling
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home at her kitchen table
